mcqs.question: Why is O(log n) considered a meaningful memory budget for class L, rather than an arbitrary small number?
options: Because log n space is enough to store a full copy of any input of size n
Because log n space guarantees the algorithm also runs in constant time
Because log n bits is exactly enough to store a constant number of pointers/indices into an input of size n, without room to copy the input itself
Because it's simply the smallest space bound anyone has studied
mcqs.explanation: An index into an array of n elements needs about log n bits to represent, so O(log n) space allows a constant number of such pointers/counters — enough to track position while scanning input — but not enough to store a copy of the input, which would need O(n) space. This is exactly why L-class algorithms are structured around scanning with pointers rather than building auxiliary data structures the size of the input.

mcqs.question: We know L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE. What is the current state of knowledge about whether any of these are STRICT subset relationships?
options: All of them have been proven strict
None of the containments are proven strict anywhere in the chain
It has been proven that all five classes are actually equal
Every containment except L ⊂ PSPACE (the endpoints) remains open; L is proven strictly smaller than PSPACE via the space hierarchy theorem
mcqs.explanation: The space hierarchy theorem proves L ⊂ PSPACE is strict (more space provably allows solving more problems), but the intermediate boundaries — including the famous P vs NP question — remain unresolved open problems. It's neither the case that everything is proven strict nor that everything is proven equal; it's a specific, known exception (the endpoints) amid broad open questions in the middle.
